ch13.anchor: Ren Bishi was born Ren Peiguo
ch13.note: Ren Bishi (1904–1950), born in Xiangyin, Hunan, was one of the Chinese Communist Party's foremost early leaders. Elected to the provisional Political Bureau in 1927 at the age of twenty-three, he became after 1945 one of the Party's 'Five Secretaries' alongside Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, and Zhu De, the youngest of the five; he died of a cerebral hemorrhage in 1950. His birth year and birthplace and the fact of his being the youngest Political Bureau member are corroborated by his standard biography.

There is no February 30. The impossible date is the source's—whether a slip of Mu Xin's or of the meeting record he draws on—and is reproduced here as printed rather than silently corrected.

International Red Aid (from its Russian acronym MOPR) was founded by the Communist International in 1922 as a kind of 'political Red Cross,' giving legal and material aid to political prisoners and their families; its Chinese arm was the Relief Society (Jinanhui). The existence and purpose of the body are corroborated; the specific figure of 8,000 yuan rests on the Party minutes the author cites.
Author's note. Zhou Punong (oral account), 'The Unforgettable Thirty-Nine Days,' Zhejiang Qingnian, 1982, no. 12.

ch13.anchor: Guan Xiangying was born Guan Zhixiang
ch13.note: Guan Xiangying (1902–1946), a Manchu of the Gūwalgiya clan born near Dalian, later served as political commissar to He Long—in the Second Front Army on the Long March and in the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army. His birth date, ethnicity, clan, and the offices traced in this sketch match the independent record.
Author's note. Zhang Ji'en, 'Fragments of Comrade Zhou Enlai's Revolutionary Activity in Shanghai, and Other Matters,' Shanghai Dangshi Ziliao Congkan, 1979, no. 1.

ch14.anchor: also known by his courtesy name Yang Xizi
ch14.note: Yang Du (1874/75–1931), of Xiangtan, Hunan, was one of modern China's most striking political reversals. A monarchist theorist, he headed the Peace Planning Society (Chou'an hui) in 1915 urging Yuan Shikai to take the throne, and was reckoned first of its 'Six Gentlemen'; after Yuan's fall he moved toward the revolution and, in 1929, secretly joined the Chinese Communist Party, sponsored by Zhou Enlai. He died in 1931. His Party membership stayed little known until Zhou Enlai, months before his own death in 1975, had it entered in the Cihai (see below). His joining the Party in 1929 and his death in 1931 are corroborated; the 1975 disclosure rests on the account of Wang Yeqiu, quoted later in this chapter.

ch14.anchor: He went to study in Japan in 1920
ch14.note: The source's '1920' cannot be right: Yang Du was an anti-Qing activist well before the dynasty fell in 1911, and the Cihai entry quoted later in this same chapter gives 1902. Yang Du went to Japan in 1902. The body's figure is rendered here as printed, with the discrepancy flagged.

ch14.anchor: Du Yuesheng, the great hoodlum boss of Shanghai
ch14.note: Du Yuesheng (1888–1951), boss of Shanghai's Green Gang, rose from the opium and protection rackets of the French Concession to become the city's most powerful gangster. On Chiang Kai-shek's behalf he set up the strike-breaking China Mutual Advancement Society, had the Communist labor leader Wang Shouhua murdered on the night of 11 April 1927, and took a leading part in the massacre of Communists and workers that opened on 12 April. The account given here is corroborated by independent scholarship.

ch14.anchor: knew the politicians of the Political Study Clique well
ch14.note: Author's note. The Political Study Clique was a far-right political faction formed in 1916 out of a section of the Progressive Party and a section of the Kuomintang, given to opportunism among the Northern warlords in the scramble for office. During the Northern Expedition of 1926–1927 part of it—pro-Japanese men of the stamp of Huang Fu, Zhang Qun, and Yang Yongtai—began to collude with Chiang Kai-shek, using their reactionary political experience to help him build a counter-revolutionary regime.

ch14.anchor: a link to the Kuomintang Reorganizationists
ch14.note: Author's note. After the Kuomintang was reorganized in 1924, its right wing, headed by Hu Hanmin, opposed Sun Yat-sen's new policies. After the right assassinated Liao Zhongkai in August 1925, Hu Hanmin was forced to flee and the right's power in Guangzhou was struck a blow. At that time fourteen men—Xie Chi, Zou Lu, Lin Sen, Ju Zheng, Dai Jitao, Ye Chucang, Shi Qingyang, Shao Yuanchong, Shen Dingyi, Zhang Ji, Wu Jingheng (Zhihui), Qin Zhen, Fu Rulin, and Mao Zuquan—held, of their own accord, a Fourth Plenary Session of the Central Executive Committee before Sun Yat-sen's coffin at the Biyun Temple in the Western Hills of Beijing (the Kuomintang's first Central Executive Committee numbered twenty-four in all; eight took part in the Western Hills meeting, two of the rest were central supervisory members and four alternate supervisory members), and set up a rival Center in Shanghai, becoming known as the 'Western Hills Conference faction.'
In July 1917 the warlord Zhang Xun briefly restored the deposed Qing boy-emperor Puyi to the throne in Beijing. The restoration collapsed within a fortnight.

ch14.anchor: a secret member of the Communist Party
ch14.note: Author's note. Yin Qi, Pan Hannian de qingbao shengya [Pan Hannian's Career in Intelligence] (People's Publishing House, 1976), 63–64.
Qi Baishi (1864–1957) was among the most celebrated Chinese painters of the twentieth century.

The Cihai ('Sea of Words') is the standard large-scale Chinese encyclopedic dictionary, first published in 1936 and reissued in revised editions; an entry in it carries a kind of official standing, which is why the matter of Yang Du mattered.
Author's note. Wang Yeqiu, 'An Unforgettable Memory,' Renmin Ribao, 30 July 1978.

ch14.anchor: Hu Egong asked that Yang Xianzhen be sent
ch14.note: Yang Xianzhen (1896–1992) later headed the Party's Higher Party School and became a leading Marxist philosopher; in 1964 he was publicly denounced for his thesis that 'two combine into one,' condemned as a metaphysical challenge to the dialectical 'one divides into two.' Here he is a young intelligence assistant at the outset of an underground career that would open, within weeks, with his arrest in Beiping.
